thread.title: Fossil: Classic Case Of Too Far, Too Fast - Fossil, Inc. (NASDAQ:FOSL)

author: Michael Boyd
title: Fossil: Classic Case Of Too Far, Too Fast - Fossil, Inc. (NASDAQ:FOSL)
text:
The turnaround in Fossil ( FOSL ) equity pricing has been a breathtaking one to observe. Left for dead by the Street just a few quarters ago, investors have suddenly come around to the company off the back of what were viewed as two strong quarters… despite poor bottom line results. As I spoke about in bearish Fossil coverage back late in 2016 , management has a history of overpromising and underdelivering, overestimating their own brand value and ability to generate economic profitable margin. Wearables growth has been built off of a base of next to zero, but corporate strategy there has been one built around generating hundreds of different SKUs, seeing what sticks in the consumer's mind. This has created inventory problems and a culture of promotional pricing in the past, and is likely to do so again. Heavily reliant on licensing deals that leverage the value of other brand names versus their own, and pressured by a continued shift towards lower margin wearables, in my opinion Fossil expectations have once again flown too high.
Bears, which held the majority of the float short, simply got too greedy at the bottom. Covering those short positions has been a large driver of the rally. While Fossil has a path to profitability and did not deserve to be valued nearly at the cash value of its balance sheet, significant risks remain. The company is priced nearly at perfection today, and while it might see some further upside as the sell-side frantically revises price targets upwards and moves more institutional investors back into the name, I do not believe $30.00/share is anywhere near fair value.
Business Overview, Licensing Risks Fossil is a global seller of consumer fashion accessories: watches, jewelry, handbags, leather goods, and sunglasses. However, fundamentally Fossil is a watch company. 79% of fiscal 2017 sales were generated from watch sales and all of the growth at the company since 2010 has come from this category – not leather goods or jewelry. In fiscal 2010, $611mm in sales were generated outside of watches; that figure had fallen to $589mm by fiscal 2017. This means that more than $700mm in growth over those years has come from growth in the watch category, a key fact investors have to keep this in mind when evaluating whether there is a bottom in watches after mid-single digit constant currency revenue declines in both fiscal 2016 and 2017.
Setting the focus on watches aside for one moment, the consumer retail accessory business has historically carried higher margin than other areas of retail. Companies do this by leveraging brand reputation. While management is a believer in the value of its Fossil brand name as “an American vintage-inspired aspirational lifestyle brand” ( Fiscal 2017 Form 10-K , Page 2), the company also licenses the rights to use other recognizable retail names like Tory Burch, Marc Jacobs, Michael Kors, and Diesel. Reliance on licensed product revenue has increased materially in recent years, now generating nearly 50% of total company revenue by utilizing its supply chain to produce product. Shareholders need to be honest here: the company uses licensing agreements because its own brand does not carry the same clout.Licensing agreements carry costs – I estimate royalty payments of $170mm in 2018 – that run at ~13% of revenue generated off the sale. That is a substantial cut, with third parties being very sensitive to failure to meet sales thresholds. The expiry of licensing agreements, and associated termination clauses, are major hurdles for Fossil on a go forward basis. Given Fossil has had a history of very favorable royalty terms, the renegotiation or potential early termination of these agreements should be forefront on shareholder minds.
After all, that reality is a large reason why Fossil already lost licensing rights with Adidas and Burberry last fiscal year. Of the remaining partners, Michael Kors and Armani represent 34.5% of consolidated sales and nearly three quarters of licensed product revenue. While these contracts are in place through 2024 and 2025 respectively, both entities have the right to terminate early if certain sale thresholds are not met. The company does not break down sales comps by licensor, however the company did note that Michael Kors (22.6% of consolidated revenue) had the most significant decline in fiscal 2017 (2017 Form 10-K, Page 38). Continued weak comps could lead to pressure. Investors should note that Michael Kors has guided same store sales comps flat for its fiscal 2019. Michael Kors is now a very mature brand, with management focused on nurturing recently acquired Jimmy Choo. Because of this, prior tailwinds from cross company benefits (Fossil generating higher sales due to strong interest from consumers buying more Michael Kors products) is now unlikely.
Excessive Promotional Activity, Nuance To The Watch Business Understanding Fossil’s place in this market is based upon understanding consumer demand behind the watch category. This is not just about the advent of smart watches (“wearables”) but also the company’s position in traditional watch business as well. For the latter, unfortunately Fossil has historically mismanaged its business, destroying any and all brand desirability by selling not just through Fossil retail stores, but also wholesale through bottom of the barrel retailers like Kohl’s ( KSS ), Wal-Mart ( WMT ), and JC Penney ( JCP ). Time and again, retailers that take this approach to leverage off of a spark in initial consumer interest. In fiscal 2010, the company operated 93 outlet stores and 230 U.S. retail stores. Operating margin was 18.5% on $2,031mm in revenue. Fast forward to fiscal 2017, the company had nearly tripled its outlet store base (273) even after closing 33 outlet stores during the year. Investors should note that total open full price retail store count had barely changed over this period. Operating margin, excluding $48mm in restructuring charges and a $407mm impairment charge, was barely positive despite significantly higher sales versus fiscal 2010. Shareholders can blame more licensed products, more discounting, and a larger percentage of direct to consumer sales which still carry lower margins.
Many of these mistakes are made quite often in luxury retail, lessons that Coach (now Tapestry ( TPR )), Kate Spade, and many other retailers in this space have learned recently. It is easy for senior executives to do to create a spark of earnings, but the damage can take years to undo. Fossil is predominantly selling “fashion” watches, leveraging its own brand name, as well as the others it licenses, to sell cheaply made products at premium prices. That isn’t a crime or a reason to short; gross margins are high on many luxury goods. However, given Fossil’s damage to its brand by heavy promotional discounting, as well as the nature of the watch market, investors have reason to take pause.
Fossil describes the watch category as having four segments (fine watches, designer watches, mass market, fashion), stating that it competes in all four segments. Before touching that, I believe it is important to break the distinction first between mechanical and quartz movements, or what powers the actual time-keeping mechanism. Mechanical watches have intricate arrangements of wheels, jewels, and winding mechanisms to tell time via mechanical movement. All of the high-end luxury brands (Rolex, Patek Philippe, Piguet) utilize mechanical movements.
Mechanical watches, especially those where the movements are made in house, create consumer desire through ties to history and craftsmanship. These movements, even separated from the actual watch itself, sell for thousands of dollars and are a large reason why these premiere (historically Swiss) brands retain their value or in some cases increase with time.
On the other hand, quartz watches are battery powered. There is no pedigree or skill associated with their production. Fossil watches are predominantly assembled in China, with the company sourcing components (cases, crystals, dials, movements) from outside vendors. Even Fossil’s high end line – Michele – does not retain value . The moment a customer leaves the store after purchasing, these watches are worth 80% less – if they carry any value at all. That is not a recipe for success. When investors think about all of the truly successful sellers of consumer discretionary products (Apple ( AAPL ), Nike ( NKE ), or even other watchmakers like Movado ( MOV ) or Swatch Group ( OTCPK:SWGAY ) through its better brands (Tissot, Longines, Omega, Rado)), trends in resale and retained value is generally indicative of a better run business.
This ties into wearables. As management has stated often, their goal is to get back to net growth in watches in total, with consistent declines in the traditional watch business eventually being offset by wearables. Gross margins are historically much lower by 1000bps, an important factor when considering the low margins that Fossil has historically operated at. Management views this as less of a problem as wearables traditionally carry a higher price point. In other words, selling one watch with 40% gross margin at $400 is better than selling two watches at 50% gross margin for $150 per. I’m not sure how much of a market exists for low technology, fake fashion watches. Apple ( AAPL ), Samsung ( OTC:SSDIY ), and Garmin ( GRMN ) have been, and likely will continue, to dominate technology-driven smartwatch markets. Traditional watchmakers, too, could make entry into these segments given their better access to capital; Tag Hauer and others have made this step. For those that don’t want an outdated watch and a timeless piece, traditional higher end watches will remain the mainstay. In my view, Fossil’s wearables have a high likelihood of cannibalizing its own traditional quartz watch sales.
Long term guidance has historically been that top line contraction will occur – once again – in fiscal 2018, stabilize in 2019, and return to growth in 2020. While management touts massive growth figures from its wearables lines, at less than 20% of total sales these watches only grew $50mm year over year. That still was not good enough to offset annual declines in the portfolio. Meanwhile, the wholesale business continued to contract in the low double digits. The problem is not sales – it is the margin profile. Management believes it can return to double digit operating margin over time, to a large extent due to taking out $200mm in cost. The problem is management has been talking about this for some time. See the below from the Q4 2016 conference call nearly eighteen months ago:
We believe that we can return to low-teen operating margins in the future, and our ability to do that turns principally on three key factors. First is New World Fossil. As you know, the financial goal of the program is to improve profitability by at least $200 million over time, and we'll invest up to $150 million in one-time cost to drive that annuity. We're still in the very early stages of the program, but we've already made great progress.
Today, view signs of that are to be found within reported results, although Fossil has stated $80mm has been realized out of that goal. Taken at word, the entirety of GAAP operating results improvement in Q1 2018 ($19mm loss versus $7mm loss, excluding restructuring charges) has been by cost take-out rather than any improvement in the business. This all comes down to the shift from higher margin activity into lower margin activity.
Backwards-Looking Free Cash Flow, Levered Balance Sheet Many investors pointed towards strong free cash flow last year in support of future growth, highlighting the excellent free cash flow yield. As is all too commonplace, investors are pulling forward unrepeatable results. Of the $180mm in GAAP operating cash flow booked last year, $155mm was driven by positive working capital changes. Making matters worse in my eyes, most of this was done by stretching out liabilities (accounts payable, accrued expenses) rather than making progress on running a better business on the assets side (lower inventory, reduced receivables).
The unsustainability of this was made apparent in Q1 2018, when Fossil reported a $4mm cash from operations loss versus $51mm positive in Q1 2017. Compared to luxury retail comps (Movado, Tapestry, Michael Kors, Restoration Hardware ( RH ), others), inventory turnover is already better than peer averages. Versus its own history, current working capital of $633mm is now well below the $900-1,000mm range that was common place from fiscal 2014 to fiscal 2017. It is unlikely that investors will see meaningful tailwinds to cash balance due to these factors this year. With sell-side expectations of adjusted earnings per share of $0.40 for fiscal 2018, as well as term loan amortization, it is unlikely that Fossil generates any meaningful cash flow, especially when viewed against the $1,500mm market cap.
Taking the mid-point of current fiscal 2018 guidance as factual (2.5% operating margin, 8.5% sales decline), the company will generate $182mm (not backing out stock-based compensation, Revolver allows the exclusion). I’m less concerned on the revenue line and more on whether or not Fossil can turn back around to generating positive margin. In Q1 of 2018, even excluding restructuring charges, that was not there. Like many retailers, Q4 will be make or break and I do not believe anyone can draw solid conclusions on how strong the watch business – smart watches or not – will be in the holiday season.
Given the probable lack of free cash flow in fiscal 2018, investors should pay attention to leverage. Fossil held $463mm in gross debt at the end of Q1. As defined under the credit agreement, total indebtedness includes all indebtedness, excluding $75mm for capital and synthetic leases and is not net of cash. For those unaware, ASU 2016-02, an accounting standard set by the Financial Accounting Standards Board (“FASB”), will bring operating leases on balance sheet by calendar year 2019. With $175mm in operating lease expense likely in fiscal 2019, covenant-defined leverage is around 2.8x dependent on letters of credit. Lenders already got more aggressive during the last refinance, with the total credit commitment reduced to $850mm, capital expenditures restricted to $35mm, higher interest rates on the base rate and LIBOR rate loans, added monthly forced amortization (further reducing true free cash flow), and tightened the consolidated total leverage ratio (3.5x by September 2019). Keeping abreast of that gross debt covenant is a large reason why Fossil paid down net debt recently out of its cash balances. If (or when) Fossil runs into problems, it has limited flexibility to tackle them.
Takeaway The terms of the company’s loan agreements restrict Fossil’s ability to invest in its business meaningfully or to change direction. While results did meaningfully improve as far as wearables uptake, I do not believe investors should be content that the status quo of Q1 run-rate (with the big question mark surrounding the holiday season) is good enough to justify the current $1,500mm market cap valuation. Several concerns remain beyond the terms of the credit facility: lack of free cash flow, history of excess promotional activity, and a “cut to prosperity” mindset. While there is likely to be some tailwinds to the share price as investment banks hit the upgrade button to keep up with the share price (see Keybanc) and the company talks its book through Q2, I’m not sold that the back half of fiscal 2018 goes as well as management and shareholders believe. If I were a shareholder, I’d be wiping my brow and moving on. North of $40.00/share, regardless of momentum, I’d be a willing short.
